analysis.title: EcoWeek 26.39: Why China resists rebalancing its growth model?
key_insights: China's growth slowed to 4.6% y/y over the first three quarters of 2026, from 5.0% in 2025. Domestic demand is weak while exports, driven by AI equipment and green technologies, are very strong.

Household demand is under pressure from a property crisis now in its sixth year and a sluggish labour market. Bank loans to households fell 1% y/y, house sales continue to fall and retail sales are stagnating.
Goods exports rose 21.9% y/y in USD over the first nine months of 2026, against 5.2% in 2025. AI-related goods exports rose 55.8% y/y. China's export market share held at 14.6% in H1 2026.
Net exports are expected to contribute about a third of China's real GDP growth in 2026, as in 2024-2025.

China's trade surplus reached a record USD1,249 billion over the twelve months to September 2026, three times its 2019 level. The 2026 current account surplus is expected to approach a record USD800 billion, nearly 4% of GDP and 0.6% of global GDP.
Imports rose 27.2% y/y over the first nine months of 2026. Commodity exporters and Asian AI value-chain producers, notably South Korea, benefit.
The yuan's real effective exchange rate remains 10% below its 2021 average. The IMF estimated at end-2025 that it was undervalued by 12% to 20%.

The 15th Five-Year Plan prioritises innovation, high-tech export-oriented sectors and self-reliance. Social security and consumption reforms stay on the back burner, and fiscal policy was tightened in 2026 until new Q4 measures.

Beijing resists rebalancing because exports support growth, assert technological and industrial supremacy, and offset a shrinking labour force. Expanding the social safety net conflicts with fiscal prudence and strained local government finances. The household savings rate was 35.7% of disposable income in 2025.
Industrial profits recovered in 2026 but are concentrated in AI-related sectors. 30% of industrial companies report losses, versus 26% in 2022.

The US and EU absorbed 24% and 28% of China's trade surplus over the last twelve months. US-China tensions could rise again in 2027 when the current truce ends. The EU is moving to more targeted restrictions.

BNP sees a concerted Plaza-style adjustment as unlikely and a yuan revaluation alone as of limited effect. China can ease tensions in the short term by investing more abroad. Structural change is feasible only when Beijing judges the costs of its export model exceed the strategic gains.

Global markets saw a tech stock selloff, which drove safe-haven flows into US Treasuries, JGBs and bunds and lowered yields despite energy prices near spring highs. Brent touched $117/b, near its April peak. TTF gas rose to 97 EUR/MWh, its highest since Dec 2022.

The French 10-year spread over Germany peaked at 174 bps on Friday, the highest since 2011 and 16 bps short of its all-time high. The 10Y yield briefly exceeded 5.1%. Moody's kept France at Aa3 with a negative outlook, conditional on adopting a deficit-reducing budget.
The Fed, ECB and BOJ are expected to be on hold next week while signalling further rate action is likely.
UK September CPI was 3.5% y/y against consensus 3.4%, its highest in 11 months. Core CPI was 2.8%. UK PPI was 8.3% y/y.
Eurozone flash composite PMI fell to 51.9 (-1.2 m/m). France's composite PMI fell to 48.4. Eurozone consumer confidence fell to -17.9.

US housing starts fell 5.2% m/m in September, a third straight monthly decline. The 30-year mortgage rate eased to 7.32%. The OCC's final GENIUS Act rule leaves room for stablecoin customers to receive yield or rewards through third parties, effective January 18, 2027. Issuers still cannot pay holders interest solely for holding.

Central bank moves: PBoC plans to switch its key rate to the overnight reverse repo. Bank Indonesia held at 5.75% and raised its deposit facility rate to 5%. BoK held at 3.0% and may tighten. Hungary held at 5.5%. Turkey cut 100bp to 36%.
Brazil's Lula was re-elected with 51.8% of the vote. Public debt exceeds 82% of GDP.

macro_indicators.reading: 4.6% y/y over first three quarters of 2026
macro_indicators.interpretation: Growth is slowing from 5.0% in 2025, held back by weak domestic demand.
Exports are accelerating from 5.2% in 2025, led by AI-related goods at +55.8%.
Record high, three times the 2019 level, which raises friction with the US and EU.

macro_indicators.reading: approaching USD800 billion, nearly 4% of GDP
macro_indicators.interpretation: A record level, 0.6% of global GDP.
Above consensus of 3.4% on energy prices. Core CPI was 2.8%, in line.
Down 1.2 m/m but still in expansion, led by a decline in France.
Down 2.7 m/m, partly reflecting the riots.
Third consecutive monthly decline, Q3 average lowest since Q2 2020.
Highest in 3.5 years on energy and metals.
Underlying price pressure is rising, with the New Core at its fastest since January.
Above the 2% target, leaving the BoK room to raise rates.

crypto_views: The OCC's final GENIUS Act implementation rule allows stablecoin customers to receive yield or rewards, while issuers remain barred from paying interest solely for holding payment stablecoins. This shifts from the February proposal and renews banking industry concern about deposit flight. It takes effect January 18, 2027.
risk_factors: Rising US-China tension when the truce ends in 2027.
EU trade restrictions on Chinese goods.
Unsustainable Chinese imbalances could lead to a sudden adjustment triggered by a crisis.
Rising French fiscal and political stress, with a spread near its all-time high.
Energy price surge on possible Gulf re-escalation.
Chinese corporate stress: rising loss-making firms, payment delays and pressure on financial institutions.
Brazil's high public debt and limited fiscal room.
Rupiah pressure after MSCI's downgrade warning.
charts_described: Chart 1 plots Chinese export, import, retail sales and investment volume growth, showing solid exports and sluggish domestic demand.
Chart 2 plots the China 12-month trade balance against the REER, showing record-high surpluses and a relatively weak yuan.
Chart 3 plots social spending against R&D as % of GDP, showing R&D is a higher budget priority.
geopolitical: US-China relations are in 'strategic stability', and the current tariff truce ends in 2027.
The EU is tightening restrictions on Chinese goods and market access, especially in autos and chemicals, without decoupling.
China is adding 40 key technologies, including LLMs, computing clusters, biotech and photovoltaics, to its export-controlled list.
China uses critical materials as a bargaining chip in trade negotiations.
Rumours of imminent re-escalation of military operations in the Gulf pushed energy prices up.
Riots and demonstrations in France added to political and fiscal stress.

tension_points.bull_case: Exports drive about a third of GDP growth, keep China's market share at 14.6%, and support technological and industrial power and job creation.
tension_points.bear_case: Weak domestic demand, record surpluses, falling corporate margins, rising loss-making firms and growing intolerance from the US and EU.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A shift in the cost-benefit balance, when Beijing judges the costs of the export-led model outweigh the strategic gains, would force structural change.

theme_stances.key_argument: China's growth model is worsening external imbalances, and Beijing resists adjusting it because exports serve growth and strategic goals.
theme_stances.evidence: Beijing is not giving ground on any key issues.

theme_stances.key_argument: Markets price worst-case scenarios on French fiscal repair, though Moody's keeping its rating could marginally help stabilise the spread.
theme_stances.evidence: markets price in anticipation of worst-case scenarios
